overview: The Narragansett are a continuing Native nation of the Rhode Island region, with coastal settlements, inland resources and important relationships with neighboring peoples. Their leaders were major participants in seventeenth-century New England politics. The imported 1492 to 1500 outline is a broad ancestral-area sketch, not a modern reservation boundary or the lifetime of the nation.

sections.title: A homeland visible in material evidence

items.text: Salt Pond, archaeological site RI 110 at the head of Point Judith Pond, preserves a large coastal village dated by the state’s account to about 1100 to 1300 CE. Archaeologists found traces of houses, other structures, cooking places and food storage. These are clues to a working community, not simply isolated valuable objects.

Plant specialists found maize in five archaeological features at Salt Pond. Their 2008 study combines these remains with associated dating evidence to establish cultivation before European settlement. Charred food that survived underground can answer questions that a written visitor’s description never addressed.

A Narragansett basket dated to around 1675 survives in the Rhode Island Historical Society’s collection as 1842.2.1. Basswood splints and corn husk are combined with red wool. A later note describes a hurried gift, but the museum calls most of that story myth. The basket itself preserves evidence of careful weaving.

In 2013, Rhode Island’s transportation department purchased approximately 52 acres containing the Salt Pond site after a dispute over proposed housing. The Narragansett Tribal Historic Preservation Office participated in its protection. Archaeological knowledge here depended on decisions about roads, development and the survival of a culturally important place.

Lorén Spears describes winter villages sheltered by inland woods and located near fresh water. Summer brought movement toward bays and salt ponds. Seasonal living joined access to food, building materials and protected places, rather than keeping every household in one location year-round.

Fishing weirs guided fish into places where people could catch them. Women dried or smoked catches for later meals, while older children helped tend gardens. Seaweed and fish fertilized crops. Family food supplies depended on coordinated work on land and water.

In 1636, Canonicus and Miantanomi permitted Roger Williams to settle at Providence. Spears explains the agreement as permission to use land under Narragansett authority. Colonists’ treatment of such agreements as outright purchases helped turn diplomatic arrangements into disputes over sovereignty.

The December 1675 Great Swamp attack killed Narragansett civilians as well as fighters during the regional war. Colonists subsequently enslaved survivors, including people sent to the Caribbean. Remaining Narragansett joined with Niantic relatives and allies, rebuilding community amid devastating losses.

The Narragansett Dawn, edited by Princess Redwing and Ernest Hazard in 1935 and 1936, carried language lessons, cultural and political discussion, and news of births and deaths. Copies preserved by the University of Rhode Island show a community describing itself in print, including the everyday milestones that larger histories can overlook.

An attested modern written greeting is “Asco wequassinummis, neetompooag!” Lorén Spears translates it as “Hello my friends” at the start of her 2017 Tomaquag Museum account. This is a named Narragansett writer’s published language sample, rather than a phrase reconstructed for the map’s fifteenth-century setting.

Spears’s 2017 account of Nikommo describes a gathering with a feast, social activities and gifts for people in need. Clothing, toys and handmade items could circulate through the giveaway. The occasion connected celebration with looking after other households: sharing was part of the event itself.

A 2018 Tomaquag Museum article shows Skyla Jennings, identified as Narragansett, learning basket making in an arts-and-wellness class. Another photograph shows Lorén Spears teaching corn-husk doll making. These named examples document learning through hands and materials alongside classroom education in a modern community.

An 1882 auction broadside documents the sale of reservation land during Rhode Island’s attempt to dissolve Narragansett political status. Treating Native people as isolated individuals could make collectively held land easier to sell. The document is evidence of a state policy, not proof that the nation consented to disappear.

Narragansett people continued monthly meetings and their annual August gathering after the state’s attempted detribalization. They retained recognized leaders and raised money for land claims. These ordinary acts of meeting, contributing and choosing representatives helped sustain institutions when outsiders claimed the community had ended.

A land-claim settlement in 1978 restored approximately 1,800 acres, and federal acknowledgment followed in 1983. The tribal history also records a longhouse built in the early 1940s as a meeting place. A continuing nation needed spaces for practical government as well as ceremonies.

ending.text: Narragansett sovereignty and landholding suffered severe losses through colonial war and later state policies, but the people and their institutions continued. The map’s 1500 endpoint is only an imported coverage cutoff; federal acknowledgment in 1983 recognized an enduring community.
